accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE EYFS statutory framework (2024) ELG Self-Regulation, which asks children to wait for what they want and control their immediate impulses when appropriate, and Development Matters 2021 PSED for 3 and 4 year olds (taking turns, following rules). The distraction claim was checked against Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss (1972), where children who sang or distracted themselves waited longer; no claim is made about long-term outcomes, which later replications questioned.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-years waiting slips: grabbing or pushing in to get a go sooner, believing the child at the back never gets a turn, and asking 'Is it my go?' over and over as if that shortens the wait. Each is a prediction, a refused lab action with a reason, or a tagged challenge option.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwait has its own mechanics: a slide queue that rotates when the front child is tapped, a choice scene whose faces turn sad on grab or push, a swinging pendulum that is counted swing by swing, and a real-time sand timer that ignores early asks. No other flag lab models a queue or a timed wait; the 6-token shingle gate passed against every flag lab, including flagplay's turn-taking tower.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees the line move up one place per go until 'You' reaches the front, sees Kit's face turn sad when they grab, counts the swing up to 5 and 7 before 'My go now?' works, and asks the timer early only to find the sand unchanged. The text confirms what the queue, faces and sand already showed.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: the child at the back never gets a go (the queue proves otherwise), grabbing gets you digging faster (the scene stops the game and Kit is sad), and asking again makes the sand fall faster (the timer runs at its own speed whatever is tapped).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers: 'rude' and 'push' model asking instead, 'me' and 'ben' fix who is at the front, 'tug' and 'take' cover interrupting a grown-up or taking a snack, 'faster' and 'stops' correct the timer belief, and 'grab' and 'cry' offer counting as the strategy.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid text FK grade -1.3 and adult text FK 8.2 from learn/readability.py (limits 6.5 and 9.5). Kid sentences are a few words with Ana, Ben and Kit; adult text uses the EYFS terms self-regulation, impulse control, turn-taking and waiting strategies, and names the adult slip of open-ended waits.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matched and explanation overlap with every other lesson, including 'Playing alongside and together', stays under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph shows one situation; adult paragraphs give the goal, why waiting is hard plus the research, named mistakes with what to do instead, and the lab steps.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 Android in dark and light for all six steps. The four children in the slide line first overlapped each other and the slide at 360 px, so spacing and size were changed and rechecked; choice cards are full width, the timer and swing are centred, and the big buttons wrap below. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme; every canvas action has a big button (each child's name, the three choices, Count a swing, Turn the timer, Is it my go?, both sort boxes) and the canvas aria-label is updated with every result. Show me completes all five tasks inside the 6 second limit.

sources: DfE (2024) Statutory framework for the early years foundation stage: ELG Self-Regulation and Managing Self
DfE (2021) Development Matters: Personal, Social and Emotional Development (3 and 4 year olds)
Mischel, W., Ebbesen, E. B. and Zeiss, A. R. (1972) Cognitive and attentional mechanisms in delay of gratification, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 21(2)
